lawyer:
MA Matin with MA Jabbar, Advocates ----- For the Petitioner. 
Zakir Ahmed with Mrs. Masuma Akhter, Advocates ----- For Opposite Party No. 5
parties:
Asim Ali ----- Petitioner
Vs
 Badaruddin @ Suruj Mia & others ----- Opposite Parties
full_judgment:
The opposite parties 1-5 as plaintiffs instituted the above title suit for specific performance of a contract alleging, inter alia, that the suit land with an area of 0'27 acre belonged to one Musim Ali, proforma-defendant No. 3 who sold the same to this petitioner-defendant No. 1 Asim Ali and proforma defendant No. 2 Moyenuddin for a consideration of Taka 900.00 only by a registered kabala dated 31.3.69; that the defendant petitioner and the said defendant Moyenuddin executed and registered an ekrarnama in favour of the said vendor Musim Ali, proforma defendant No. 3 on the same date to the effect that if the said vendor Musim Ali would pay back the above consideration money to the vendees i.e. defendant petitioner and Moyenuddin (Defendant No. 2) within 25 years, they would execute and register a kabala of reconveyance in favour of the said vendor Musim Ali. Further case of the plaintiffs-opposite parties was that they purchased by a registered deed dated 28.3.75 the right of re-purchase from the said Musim Ali, the proforma defendant No. 3 for a consideration of (Taka 5,000.00–Taka 900.00 = Taka 4,100.00) and accordingly asked the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 to execute and register the necessary deed of reconveyance of the land in their favour. Defendant No. 2 however executed and registered a kabala on his behalf in favour of the plaintiffs for half of the lands for a consideration of Tk. 450.00 but defendant No. 1 refused to do so. Hence the suit for specific performance of contract by the plaintiffs against him and others The petitioner as defendant No. 1 filed a written statement to contest the suit contending, inter alia, that the suit is not maintainable and the same is bad for defect of parties and also barred by limitation apart from denying all other material allegations made in the plaint. It has been further stated in the written statement that the pro-defendant No. 3 the vendor is the uterine brother of the defendant No. 1, and defendant No. 2 is the son-in-law of defendant No. 1's brother; that when defendant No. 3 sold out the suit-land to the defendant petitioner and defendant No. 2 by kabala dated 31.3.69 for a consideration of Tk. 900.00 only, the vendees i.e. defendant petitioner and defendant No. 2 also executed a registered ekrarnama for reconveyance of the suit-land in favour of the vendor, pro-defendant No. 3, on the terms that if pro-defendant No. 3 would pay back the same consideration money to them (the vendees) within 25 years, then they would execute and register a deed of reconveyance in favour of the pro-defendant No. 3. But if the original vendor pro-defendant No. 3 after his repurchase would in his term again want to sell out the same land, he must sell it out to the defendant No. 1 or his heirs for the same consideration money and to none else and vice-versa. It has been further contended by the defendant petitioner in his written statement that the pro-defendant No. 3 has had no right or authority to sell out his right of repurchase to the plaintiffs who are admittedly outsiders rather strangers to the suit-property and are not privies to the ekrarnama; hence the plaintiffs acquired no right, or interest in the suit-land by their alleged purchase of the right pf repurchase from the pro-defendant No. 3 vide Ext. 1 i.e. the deed of purchase of the right of repurchase dated 28.3.75, the same being void and illegal in view of the ekrarnama Ext. A and further it has been contended that the defendant No. 2 has had also no right to sell out his portion of the land for half of the total consideration money i.e. Tk. 450.00 to the plaintiffs in violation of the terms of the registered ekrarnama and as such the purchase of the right of repurchase from pro-defendant No. 3 as well as the purchase of half of the land from defendant No. 2 by the plaintiffs vide Ext. 1 and 1(B) respectively are all illegal and void and that the plaintiffs acquired no right or title by virtue of the said deeds. The suit is therefore liable to be dismissed with cost. 

 3. Plaintiff No. 3 only examined himself as PW 1 on behalf of all the plaintiffs and the contesting defendant No. 1 examined himself as the only DW in support of their respective cases. The learned Munsif upon consideration of the pleadings framed the following issues: 

 4. The learned Munsif decided issue Nos. 2 and 3 in favour of the plaintiffs. Then he took up the issue Nos. 1, 4 and 5 together for convenience of discussion and on consideration of the facts of the case and the evidence on record and the relevant provisions of law came to the finding that the vendor pro-defendant No. 3 has had no right to transfer his above conditional right of repurchase to any 3rd party, here the plaintiffs, who are outsiders and not privies to the ekrarnama. So, the transfer of the ekrar-right by the proforma defendant No. 3 to the plaintiffs by a kabala executed and registered on 28.3.75 (Ext.1) was wholly bad and illegal, being in violation of the terms of the ekrarnama Ext. A. The very ekramama did not provide him i.e. pro-defendant No. 3 with any such right of retransfer of his right of repurchase to any 3rd party except the defendants Nos. 1 and 2 or their legal heirs. As the very transfer of the right of repurchase by pro-defendant No. 3 was void and illegal, the subsequent transferees i.e. plaintiffs of this suit did not acquire any valid right, or interest from proforma defendant No. 3 vide kabala dated 28.3.75 (Ext. 1). Moreover, the terms and conditions of the said ekrarnama (Ext A) equally bound the defendant No. 2 and as such he was also not competent to transfer his share of the lands to any 3rd party like the plaintiffs other than the proforma defendant No. 3 or defendant No. 1 or their heirs. So, the transfer of the half of the suit land to the plaintiffs by the defendant No. 2 vide kabala dated 3.4.75 Ext. 1(B) was also void and illegal and hence the plaintiffs acquired no right, title in the suit-land thereby. The learned Munsif therefore dismissed the suit on contest without cost against the defendant No. 1 and ex parse against the rest by his judgment and decree dated 12.12.77. 

 8. Mr. Matin, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, has firstly taken me through the judgments of both the courts below and some other relevant papers on record and then seriously assailed the judgment of the court of appeal below. His submission is that the learned Subordinate Judge has committed gross error of law apparent on the face of the record in reversing the judgment and decree of the trial Court and decreeing the suit absolutely on misconception and misconstruction of the relevant provisions of law and the connected documents particularly the ekrarnama Ext. A and this has resulted in a failure of justice and as such the impugned judgment and decree of the Court of appeal below are bad and illegal and the same should be set aside, His further contention is that the learned Subordinate Judge has misread the evidence as well as the material document in this case namely Ext. A, the ekrarnama and also the decision reported in 15 DLR 634 and come to an erroneous finding to the effect that the pro-defendant No. 3 has legally transferred his right of re-purchase to the plaintiffs by a kabala dated 28.3.75 Ext. 1 and the defendant No. 2 has also legally transferred his share of the suit-land to the plaintiffs by way of reconveyance by kabala Ext. I(B), and most erroneously reversed the findings and decision of the trial Court and decreed the suit, hence the aforesaid findings and the impugned judgment and decree of the Court of appeal below are liable to be set aside. It has been further contended by the learned Advocate for the petitioner that the court of appeal below has committed error of law apparent on the face of the record in not holding that the Kabala dated 31.3.69 did not create any absolute interest in favour of the vendees defendant Nos. 1 and 2, rather it was transfer by way of sale with an encumbrance and as such section 11 of the Transfer of Property Act has no manner of application to the facts of the present suit Lastly, it has been contended by the learned advocate for the petitioner that the plaintiffs-opposite parties have not come with clean hands as they have collusively tried to enter into the suit-land knowing fully that the same has been clearly intended to be kept confined within the family of the vendor and the vendees as per the ekrarnama and as such the reliefs under section 22 of the Specific Relief Act which are discretionary should not be allowed, but he refused to the plaintiffs in the facts and circumstances of the case and accordingly the suit be dismissed. 

 9. Let me now examine the above submissions of the learned Advocate for the petitioner vis-a-vis the facts of the case and the evidence on record and the relevant provisions of law on the subject. It appears from the judgments of the courts below that both the sides have relied on a decision in the case of Ratesh Chandra Mridha Vs. Hara Krishna Goldar and others, reported in 15 DLR 634. The trial Court found that no absolute interest was created in favour of the vendees defendant Nos. 1 and 2 by the sale vide kabala dated 31.3.69 by the proforma defendant No.3 in view of the fact that the deed of sale made by proforma defendant No. 3 in favour of the vendees defendant Nos. 1 and 2 was with an encumbrance, created by the ekrarnama Ext. A of the same date. The learned advocate has further contended that in the instant case, the vendor has not restricted the vendees in the suit-land in their purchase, but the vendees restricted themselves in the enjoyment of their absolute right in the lands in question by putting a restriction on its transfer to any 3rd party other than the pro-defendant No. 3 and vice-versa by execution of the said ekrarnama Ext. A in favour of the vendor i.e. pro-defendant No. 3 thereby made the right of repurchase assigned to the pro-defendant No. 3 unassignable to any outsider and hence this case does not fall within the mischief of section 11 of the Transfer of Property Act. The appellate Court, on the other hand, observed that in the instant case in the ekrarnama Ext. A, so far the words, “প্রকাশ থাকা আবশ্যক ........................ বিক্রয় করিব বা করিবে”are concerned, directed, that such interest shall be applied or enjoyed in a particular manner, The pro-defendant No. 3 here was entitled to receive and dispose of such interest as if there were no such direction, in view of section 11 of the Transfer of Property Act. So, section 11 of the Transfer of Property Act goes in favour of the pro-defendant No. 3 and the plaintiffs and not in favour of the defendant No. 1. The learned Subordinate Judge further observed that the restriction imposed and introduced in the ekrarnama is hit by section 11 of the Transfer of Property Act and as such void and that the right of repurchase of the defendant No. 3 according to the ekrarnama is assignable in view of' the decision reported in 15 DLR 634 and the plaintiffs have rightly purchased the right of repurchase from the proforma defendant No. 3 vide Ext. 1. Now, the learned Advocate for the defendant petitioner, while elaborating his points for argument has drawn my attention first to section 6(d) of the Transfer of Property Act which reads thus: 

 Section 10. Where property is transferred subject to a condition or limitation absolutely restraining the transferee or any person claiming under him from parting with or disposing of his interest in the property, the condition of limitation is void, except in the case of a lease where the condition is for the benefit of the lessor or those claiming under him: Provided that property may be transferred to or for the benefit Of a woman (not being a Hindu, Muhammadan or Buddhist). So that she shall not have power during her marriage to transfer or charge the same or her beneficial interest therein. 

 10. Now, in the instant case, it appears that the lower appellate Court has failed to carefully consider the conditions of the ekrarnama which are, in my view, not hit by any of the above sections namely sections 10 or 11 of the TP Act. Similarly, section 14 of the said Act has no application, the transfer being not in perpetuity. The lower appellate Court, of course has held that the conditions of the ekrarnama are hit by the above provisions of law and the right of repurchase of the vendor as per ekrarnama is assignable. But on scrutiny of the relevant sale deed and the ekrarnama in the light of provisions of the concerned laws, it appears to me that the trial Court has rightly held that the right of repurchase as in this case is not assignable or transferable and the ekrarnama is not a deed of conveyance. It is at best an agreement between the vendor and the vendees which by itself does not create any interest in the land and as such the restriction imposed in the ekrarnnama is quite valid and lawful one. But the lower appellate Court took a wrong view to the effect that the condition or the restriction in the ekrarnama is hit by sections 10 and 11 of the said Act and is void and, that the right of repurchase given to the vendor pro-defendant No.3 by the said ekrarnama is assignable or transferable to any person by him and hence the purchase of that right by the plaintiffs by the deed dated 28.3.75 vide Ext. 1 is legal and valid and in taking the above view, the learned Subordinate Judge has also relied on the decision reported in 15 DLR 634 and has quoted in his impugned judgment from the above decision that the right to a vendor of immovable property on the basis of an agreement to transfer by the vendee at the time of sale is assignable. But Mr. Matin has pointed out that the learned Subordinate Judge has taken a partial and one-sided view of the decision cited above and has failed to notice some very material portion of the said decision and thereby has fallen in serious error of law in relying upon the same. The learned Advocate has then drawn my attention to the relevant portion of the said decision in paragraph 7 which may be quoted as follows: 

 "In the former case Chief Justice Beaumont held that both under the common Law and section 23(b) of the Specific Relief Act an option to repurchase property is prima facie assignable, though it may be so worded as to show that it was to be personal to the grantee and not assignable. In that case the vendee contracted to payoff the money and convey back to the vendor a part of the property. It was held that an agreement for sale or repurchase of immovable property is a contract and that benefit under a contract could be assigned, unless performance depends upon something personal or special." 

 Mr. Matin has pointed out that portion of the decision as under-lined above which escaped the notice of the learned Subordinate Judge and thereby he committed the mistake by taking a wrong view. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has further submitted that the ekrarnama is at best a contract and its performance depends upon something personal or special to the effect that in case of reconveyance by the vendees to the vendor according to the ekrarnama, Ext. A, it shall be confined within the vendor and the vendees and their legal heirs at the fixed consideration of Taka 900.00 only within the period of 25 years and not to any other outsider or 3rd party and again in the case of reconveyance by the vendor in favour of the vendees as per terms of the ekrarnama, the vendor cannot but reconvey the said land for the same consideration of Tk. 900.00 to the vendee or his heirs. Of course there is no clear and express term in the ekrarnama that the vendor cannot alienate the suit-land at all, It has been stipulated that the vendor shall have a right of repurchase from the vendees at the same consideration, but if he requires to reconvey the land again he must reconvey it to the vendee or his heirs and not to any 3rd party having no privy to the ekrarnama. Hence, the performance of the ekrarnama is something personal and special in the instant case and therefore its right of repurchase or reconveyance is not and cannot be assignable and it has been rightly contended that the right of repurchase allegedly acquired by the plaintiffs vide kabala dated 28.3.75 (Ext. 1) is illegal and void and similarly the alleged purchase by the plaintiffs of the half share of the suit land from defendant No.2 who is a party to the ekrarnama is also hit by the restriction imposed by the ekrarnama i.e. the assigning of the right of repurchase to any 3rd party is illegal and void. In support of his contention, the learned Advocate for the petitioner has relied on a number of decisions, one of which is in the case of Debi Dayal Vs. Ghasita and others reported in AIR 1929 Allahabad 668 wherein it has been observed by their Lordships as follows: 

 In another decision in the case of Ughandi Mudali Vs. Regav(lchari and others reported in 1906 lLR VoL 29 Madras 307, it has been observed, "that the right conferred by the agreement was personal and not transferable." Yet another decision in the case of Muhammad Reza and others Vs. Abbas Bandi Bibi reported in 1931-32 Law Reports Indian Appeals Vol. LIX 236, wherein it has been observed: 

 "That the alienations were invalid. Having regard to section 3 of the Oudh Laws Act, 1876, the right under the contract of 1870 were to be determined according to justice, equity and good conscience, and thereunder the restriction being partial only was not repugnant to an absolute interest. The Transfer of Property Act, 1882, section 10, recognized the validity of a partial restriction upon a power of deposition in the case of transfer inter vivos,and there is no authority that a different principle applied in India before that Act was passed. Under English Law, if that were the test, a partial restriction is not repugnant, even in the case of testamentary gift." 

 The learned Advocate has also relied on a decision in the case of Achuta Ram and others Vs. Jainandan Towary and others reported in 1926 Indian Case Vol. 96 at page 287 wherein it has been held as follows: 

 By this decision the learned Advocate wants to show that the plaintiffs admittedly are outsiders and not privies to the agreement i.e. the ekrarnama and as such they cannot enforce any right of repurchase through the ekrarnama. Now, as to the allegations of misreading the ekrarnama, the learned Advocate for the petitioner has drawn my attention to the impugned judgment wherein the learned Subordinate Judge has observed about the submission of the learned Advocate of the appellant that there is no such recital in the ekrarnama that the pro-defendant No.3 is not entitled to sell out the suit-land to any 3rd party which is also bad. The condition of the ekramama shows in clear terms that the suit property cannot be transferred or retransferred to any 3rd party except to the vendees by the vendor and to the vendor by vendees or their legal heirs and vice versa on the fixed consideration of Tk. 900.00 only within a specified period. From the ekrarnama it appears that there is no absolute bar in the matter of alienation of the suit lands, rather there is provision for alienation and realienation by the vendor and the vendees but only amongst themselves or their legal heirs and not to any outsider or 3rd party. In case of application of sections 10 and 11 of the Transfer of Property Act, it appears that the condition or limitation restraining alienation or transfer of the property by the transferee or any person claiming under him must be absolute one and in that case, of course, such condition or limitation may be void except in some other cases as defined in section 10 itself. Again according to section 11 of the said Act, the interest created in favour of the person by a transfer of the property must also be absolute one and if the terms of such transfer direct that such interest shall be applied or enjoyed by him in a particular manner, he shall be entitled to receive and dispose of such interest as if there were no such direction i.e. such term or direction shall be deemed to be non-existent and void. Here, in the instant case, firstly the transfer of the suit property by a registered deed by the vendor the defendant No.3 in favour of the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 was with an encumbrance or obligation, which obligation was created by defendant Nos. 1 and 2, the transferees themselves by execution of the ekrarnama Ext. A in favour of the transferor pro-defendant No.3. Thus it cannot be said that the transferees had acquired absolute interest in the suit property by their purchase. So, unless the interest created by any transfer is absolute one, section 11 of the Transfer of Property Act shall have no application; hence the decision cited above in 15 DLR 634 goes to support the case of the defendant petitioner and not the plaintiff opposite parties. 

 In the instant case also, by the ekrarnama an obligation has been created and annexed to the ownership of transfer under section 40 of the Act and that is why the interest created by this transaction cannot be said to be absolute one which is required as a pre-condition for application of section 11 of the Transfer of Property Act. Thus viewed carefully, it appears that the decision reported in the 15 DLR 634 goes more for the help of the defendant petitioner than for the plaintiff-opposite parties. Thus, having regard to the facts and circumstances of the case and the provisions of law and the decisions cited above, I find much substance in the contention of the learned Advocate for the petitioner and I am inclined to hold that the deeds of purchase of the plaintiffs namely Ext. 1 and Ext. 1 B are all illegal and void as the pro-defendant No. 3 as well as defendant No. 2 acted contrary to the provisions of the ekrarnama Ext. A which is binding upon them. Apart from that, section 6(b) of the Transfer of Property Act appears to be clear when it says that, "An interest in property restricted in its enjoyment to the owner personally cannot be transferred by him". In the instant case, there was restriction in the description of the suit property, as such enjoyment of the said property by the ekrarnama, i.e. a right of repurchase as created in favour of the pro-defendant No. 3 with a restriction that he has the right of alienation of the same to the defendant transferee and his heirs only and not to any other persons and that this conditional and restricted right of enjoyment cannot be transferred by him to any other 3rd person in view of the terms of the ekrarnama and the aforesaid provision of law. About the last submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner that even if the plaintiffs succeed to prove their case, yet in view of their conduct and the facts and circumstances of the case and the intention as expressed in the ekrarnama to keep the property somehow within periphery of the families of the vendor and the vendees and when admittedly the plaintiffs are outsiders, their suit for specific performance of contract should be dismissed as the reliefs under section 22 of the Specific Relief Act are discretionary one to be granted or not granted in the facts and circumstances of each case. In support of this contention, the learned Advocate for the petitioner has referred to some decisions one of which is reported in the case of H and Fabric Limited vs. Mallik Textile and others reported in 1985 BLD 271 and another in the case of Ram Chandra Das and others V.I'. Md. Khalilur Rahman reported in 37 DLR (AD) 21. Of course this point does not appear to have been raised and considered by the courts below. But I find on consideration of facts and circumstances of the case and the contentions of the parties and the materials on record that the very foundation of the plaintiffs' claim of interest and title in the suit-land on the basis of the kabala dated 28.3.75, that is the deed of purchase of the right of repurchase Ext. 1, is void and illegal and similarly the deed of purchase dated 3.4.75 vide Ext. 1(B) is also void and illegal and as such the judgment and decree of the lower appellate Court cannot be sustained and the same should be set aside and the suit be dismissed. I do not like to give much weight to the last submission of the learned Advocate for the petitioner when I have found that the two documents in dispute namely Exts. 1 and 1(B) as void and illegal, I must therefore hold that the impugned judgment and decree of the Court of appeal below suffers from serious legal infirmities and the same need be interfered with and set aside in the interest of justice.
